name: दैवासुरसम्पद्विभागयोग
teaching: Two inheritances run through every human heart: one of fearlessness, charity, and harmlessness; one of hypocrisy, arrogance, and the creed that the world is loveless and false, with desire its only law. Krishna names desire, anger, and greed as the threefold gate of self-destruction — and scripture as the lamp for telling the two inheritances apart when they speak in your own voice. Two inheritances contend in every heart. The dark one is anatomized without flinching — its creed, its monologue, its three doors — and the bright one begins where fear ends. The chapter closes by handing the seeker a measure beyond appetite.
questions: Which 'demonic' trait do you recognise not in others but in yourself, even faintly?
Desire, anger, greed — which gate stands open widest in your life right now?
When your impulses and your principles conflict, what do you actually consult?

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
अभयं सत्त्वसंशुद्धिर्ज्ञानयोगव्यवस्थितिः ।
दानं दमश्च यज्ञश्च स्वाध्यायस्तप आर्जवम्॥
verses.transliteration:
abhayaṃ sattvasaṃśuddhirjñānayogavyavasthitiḥ
dānaṃ damaśca yajñaśca svādhyāyastapa ārjavam
verses.essence: The Blessed Lord says: fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in knowledge and yoga, charity, restraint, sacrifice, study, austerity, uprightness —
verses.translation: Fearlessness, purity of heart, steadfastness in knowledge and Yoga, almsgiving, control of the senses, sacrifice, study of scriptures, austerity and straightforwardness.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + भय (fear): absence of fear
सत्त्व (mind, inner being) + संशुद्धि (thorough cleansing): purity of the inner being

anvaya.base: ज्ञानयोगव्यवस्थिति · steadiness in knowledge and yoga
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + योग (yoga, concentration) + व्यवस्थिति (steadfastness): steadfastness in knowledge and in yoga
स्व (one's own) + अध्याय (study, recitation): one's own study of the Veda

verses.explanation: The inventory of the divine endowment begins, and its first word is abhayam, fearlessness. Not bravado — the deep unafraidness of one who has nothing to protect because nothing essential can be lost. Beside it stand sattva-saṃśuddhiḥ, purity of mind, which Śaṅkara glosses as honesty in all dealings, and steadiness in knowledge and yoga: learning the truth from scripture and teacher, then making it one's own experience. Śaṅkara calls these three the principal sattvic marks. From that root grow generosity, restraint, sacrifice, study, austerity and uprightness — the list reads like what a heart does once fear stops governing it.
verses.connection: Opens the chapter's ledger of two natures: the divine endowment, listed first and at length (16.1–3).
verses.reflection: Begin at the list's beginning today: practice one hour of abhayam — acting with nothing to protect.
verses.background: Chapter 16 opens with Krishna speaking unasked, after chapter 15 ended by saying that whoever understands this teaching becomes wise. Śrīdhara explains the link: who does understand it, and who does not? To answer, Krishna sets out two natures found in people and starts listing the qualities of the divine one.
verses.hook: What qualities open the list of a godly nature?

views.text: Purity of mind means honesty: no fraud, trickery or falsehood in dealings. Jñāna is knowledge learnt from scripture and teacher; yoga makes it one's own experience through concentration. These first three are the chief sattvic marks.

Fear is the pain of foreseeing loss of what one wants or contact with what one dreads; fearlessness is its absence. Sacrifice and Vedic study are done as worship of the Lord, the Vedas being read as all about Him.
The chapter opens to sort who is fit for the knowledge just taught: the divine endowment is the qualification of the one entitled to it, the demonic marks the one who is not.
Developing sattva is the first rung of the spiritual ladder and the foundation of yoga; the divine qualities must be cultivated and the demonic abandoned.
These virtues of a saintly nature are to be cultivated as spiritual practice; fearlessness, for example, comes from detachment and surrender to God, and purity of mind from attachment to him.

verses.devanagari:
अहिंसा सत्यमक्रोधस्त्यागः शान्तिरपैशुनम् ।
दया भूतेष्वलोलुप्त्वं मार्दवं ह्रीरचापलम्॥
verses.transliteration:
ahiṃsā satyamakrodhastyāgaḥ śāntirapaiśunam
dayā bhūteṣvaloluptvaṃ mārdavaṃ hrīracāpalam
verses.essence: — harmlessness, truth, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, absence of slander, compassion toward beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty, absence of fickleness —
verses.translation: Harmlessness, truth, absence of anger, renunciation, peacefulness, absence of crookedness, compassion towards beings, non-covetousness, gentleness, modesty, absence of fickleness.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + हिंसा (harming): not harming
अ (not) + क्रोध (anger)
अ (not) + पैशुन (slander, backbiting)
अ (not) + लोलुप्त्व (greediness); an archaic shortened form of अलोलुपत्व
अ (not) + चापल (restlessness, fickleness)

verses.explanation: The list's middle section reads like a description of how it feels to be near such a person: no cutting words behind backs (apaiśunam), tenderness toward creatures (dayā bhūteṣu), mārdavam — softness — and hrī, the capacity to blush, conscience worn on the skin. The divine endowment is mostly composed of harms not done and gentleness actively present.
verses.connection: The middle of the divine list begun at 16.1, turning from inner discipline to how one treats others; 16.3 completes it.
verses.reflection: Choose three from the middle of the list today: no slander, tenderness to creatures, the capacity to blush.
verses.background: Krishna, unasked, continues the list of the divine endowment begun in 16.1 with fearlessness, charity and self-restraint. This verse carries its middle stretch: eleven qualities, from harmlessness and truth to modesty and steadiness, that shape how one treats others.
verses.hook: What further virtues belong to one born with a divine nature?

views.text: Tyāga here is renunciation in the sense of monastic giving-up, since charity was already listed; śānti is control of the mind; acāpalam is not using speech, hands and feet needlessly.
Truth is speaking what one knows for certain and what is good for others; compassion is being unable to bear another's suffering.
Takes tyāga as generosity and akrodha as no agitation of mind even when struck; notes that aloluptvam is an archaic form with a vowel dropped.
Non-violence, truthfulness and freedom from anger continue the list of saintly qualities; each, like truthfulness drawing us toward God, the Absolute Truth, helps carry the aspirant to the goal.

verses.devanagari:
तेजः क्षमा धृतिः शौचमद्रोहो नातिमानिता ।
भवन्ति सम्पदं दैवीमभिजातस्य भारत॥
verses.transliteration:
tejaḥ kṣamā dhṛtiḥ śaucamadroho nātimānitā
bhavanti sampadaṃ daivīmabhijātasya bhārata
verses.essence: — vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, absence of malice, absence of arrogance: these belong to one born to the divine endowment, Bharata.
verses.translation: Vigour, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, absence of hatred, absence of pride these belong to the one born for a divine state, O Arjuna.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + द्रोह (malice, injury)
अति (excessive) + मानिता (self-esteem): thinking oneself too worthy of honour

anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, accusative singular (agrees with सम्पदम्)
past participle, masculine, genitive singular (of one)

verses.explanation: The list's final verse opens with a balanced pair: tejas, fire — the divine nature is not meek — held beside kṣamā, the forgiveness that keeps fire from becoming cruelty. Abhijātasya, 'of one born to it': temperament deals the opening hand. But the Gita's whole arc insists the hand can be replayed — these are listed precisely so they can be cultivated.
verses.connection: Completes the divine portrait; 16.4 will need only one verse for its opposite.
verses.reflection: Hold fire and forgiveness together once today — tejas with kshama, strength that refuses cruelty.
verses.background: The list of the divine endowment reaches its last six qualities. Śrīdhara notes that with these the twenty-six qualities beginning with fearlessness are complete, and Krishna now says whom they belong to.
verses.hook: Which last qualities complete the portrait of a divine nature?

views.text: Tejas is vigour, not a glowing complexion. Kṣamā is no inner disturbance when wronged, distinct from akrodha, the calming of anger once roused. 'Born to the divine' means destined for a noble future.
Tejas is the strength that cannot be overpowered by the wicked. The divine destiny is obedience to the Lord's commands, found in those born with a leaning toward it who seek to fulfil it.
Dhṛti is a sattvic state that lifts body and senses when they sink in exhaustion, so the seeker never loses heart under trial.
The list of twenty-six divine qualities closes with vigour, forgiveness, fortitude and humility, all of which the aspirant should consciously cultivate.

verses.devanagari:
दम्भो दर्पोऽभिमानश्च क्रोधः पारुष्यमेव च ।
अज्ञानं चाभिजातस्य पार्थ सम्पदमासुरीम्॥
verses.transliteration:
dambho darpo'bhimānaśca krodhaḥ pāruṣyameva ca
ajñānaṃ cābhijātasya pārtha sampadamāsurīm
verses.essence: Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance: these, Partha, belong to one born to the demonic endowment.
verses.translation: Hypocrisy, arrogance and self-conceit, anger and also harshness and ignorance, belong to one who is born for a demoniacal state, O Partha (Arjuna).

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + ज्ञान (knowledge)

anvaya.form: past participle, masculine, genitive singular (of one)
adjective, feminine, accusative singular (agrees with सम्पदम्)

verses.explanation: Against twenty-six virtues, six vices — the asymmetry is the comment: darkness is structurally simpler than light. The six chain naturally: dambha, the performance of virtue not possessed; darpa and abhimāna, the swollen self; krodha when the world disagrees; pāruṣya, the voice gone hard; and beneath all five, ajñāna — not knowing what should and should not be done. Note what is absent: no mention of horns or hells. The demonic is a psychology, available anywhere.
verses.connection: The counter-ledger, brutally brief — and 16.5 immediately reassures the listener.
verses.reflection: Run the six-point check honestly: where does performance, swagger, or hardness of voice live in me?
verses.background: Having finished the divine endowment, Krishna turns to its opposite, the demonic endowment, the nature of the asuras (the gods' rivals). Where the divine took three verses, he names the demonic in a single verse of six traits.
verses.hook: What traits mark a person of demonic nature?

views.text: Dambha is religious ostentation. Pāruṣya is cutting speech, such as mockingly calling a blind man 'lotus-eyed'. Ajñāna is a false idea of what ought and ought not to be done.
Dambha is practising dharma to win a name for righteousness; rudeness is causing grief to good people. Asuras are those who rebel against the Lord's commands.
'Demonic' stands for both the asura and the rākṣasa natures together; these six arise in one born toward that endowment.
The demonic show outward piety without inner substance, are proud of wealth and position, angry when desires are blocked, harsh to others, and mistake wrong for right.

verses.devanagari:
दैवी सम्पद्विमोक्षाय निबन्धायासुरी मता ।
मा शुचः सम्पदं दैवीमभिजातोऽसि पाण्डव॥
verses.transliteration:
daivī sampadvimokṣāya nibandhāyāsurī matā
mā śucaḥ sampadaṃ daivīmabhijāto'si pāṇḍava
verses.essence: The divine endowment leads to liberation, the demonic to bondage, it is held. Grieve not, Pandava — you are born to the divine endowment.
verses.translation: The divine nature is deemed conducive to liberation, and the demoniacal to bondage. Grieve not, O Arjuna, thou art born with divine endowments.

anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, nominative singular (agrees with सम्पत्)
past participle, feminine, nominative singular (is held)
verb, aorist used with मा, 2nd person singular (a prohibition)

verses.explanation: The stakes named — freedom or bondage — and then the teaching pauses for tenderness: mā śucaḥ, do not grieve. Krishna has watched Arjuna silently auditing himself against both lists, and answers the unspoken dread directly: *you are of the divine*. A teacher who diagnoses the demonic in the world while reassuring the anxious student in front of him — the chapter's severity is framed, start to finish, by this kindness.
verses.connection: The pastoral hinge: Arjuna cleared by name before the dark portrait deepens.
verses.reflection: When you catch a fault in yourself today, skip the despair. Name one quality from the divine list you already practise, and lean on it.
verses.background: Both endowments have now been listed, and Krishna states where each leads. Śrīdhara says that Arjuna, hearing this, wonders anxiously which nature is his own and whether he is fit for this teaching; the second half of the verse answers that unspoken doubt.
verses.hook: Where do the divine and demonic natures each lead?

views.text: The Lord sees Arjuna silently asking 'Am I of the divine or the demonic nature?' and answers before he speaks: you are born to an illustrious future.
The divine is submission to the Lord's commands and leads to reaching Him. Arjuna is divine because he is Pāṇḍu's son, Pāṇḍu being foremost among the righteous.
The list prepares for 18.63, 'reflect fully, then act': scripture and teacher give knowledge, but the power to examine critically belongs to the pupil, and Kṛṣṇa sees it in Arjuna.
One with the divine endowment is qualified for the knowledge of truth just taught; the demonic remains forever in saṃsāra. Arjuna's anxious doubt about his own fitness is what Kṛṣṇa calms.
Demonic traits keep one bound to rebirth while divine virtues free one; even a single fault can wreck spiritual progress, so alongside devotion we must work on our character, perhaps with a diary.

verses.devanagari:
द्वौ भूतसर्गौ लोकेऽस्मिन्दैव आसुर एव च ।
दैवो विस्तरशः प्रोक्त आसुरं पार्थ मे शृणु॥
verses.transliteration:
dvau bhūtasargau loke'smindaiva āsura eva ca
daivo vistaraśaḥ prokta āsuraṃ pārtha me śṛṇu
verses.essence: Two orders of beings are created in this world: the divine and the demonic. The divine has been described at length; hear from me, Partha, of the demonic.
verses.translation: There are two types of beings in this world, the divine and the demoniacal; the divine has been described at length; hear from Me, O Arjuna, of the demoniacal.

anvaya.parts: भूत (beings) + सर्ग (creation): kinds of created beings

anvaya.form: pronoun, short genitive singular (here: from me)

verses.explanation: The transition, with its quiet arithmetic: the divine took three verses and fifteen chapters of teaching; the demonic will now receive a full anatomy — because what must be guarded against must be understood. What follows (16.7–20) is scripture's most unflinching psychological portrait: not of monsters, but of a worldview, drawn from the inside.
verses.connection: Announces the fuller account of the demonic nature that follows, from its view of the world in 16.8 to where it ends.
verses.reflection: Study the dark portrait today as a mirror-check, not a verdict on others.
verses.background: Arjuna has been reassured. The divine nature has been described at length in 16.1–3, the demonic in only one verse. Śrīdhara says Krishna now expands on the demonic so that it may be avoided entirely; this verse announces that fuller account.
verses.hook: How many kinds of beings are there in this world, by nature?

views.text: The 'two creations' are people themselves, born with divine or demonic natures, as in the Upaniṣad's two classes of Prajāpati's sons. The demonic is detailed so it may be seen and avoided.

Beings are divided at birth by the force of past karma into those who carry out the Lord's commands and those who defy them; the divine conduct of karma, jñāna and bhakti yoga has already been taught.
Says 'two' by counting the asura and rākṣasa natures as one, so this does not contradict the three natures of chapter 9.
Natures are carried from past lives; humans hold both divine and demonic traits, and in this age both live in the same heart, so Krishna describes the lower nature to help us avoid it.

verses.devanagari:
प्रवृत्तिं च निवृत्तिं च जना न विदुरासुराः ।
न शौचं नापि चाचारो न सत्यं तेषु विद्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
pravṛttiṃ ca nivṛttiṃ ca janā na vidurāsurāḥ
na śaucaṃ nāpi cācāro na satyaṃ teṣu vidyate
verses.essence: The demonic do not know the way of action nor the way of restraint. Neither purity, nor right conduct, nor truth is found in them.
verses.translation: The demoniacal know not what to do and what to refrain from; neither purity, nor right conduct nor truth is found in them.

anvaya.form: verb, perfect with present sense, 3rd person plural

verses.explanation: The diagnosis begins at the compass: pravṛtti and nivṛtti — when to act, when to refrain — the basic moral directionality every tradition teaches, simply missing. Not defied; *unknown*. And the third absence is the deepest: na satyam — truth not present in them, first as honesty, finally as any felt contact with the real. The portrait will now show what a life builds on that vacancy.
verses.connection: The account promised in 16.6 opens at the root: before any view or deed, the demonic cannot tell what to do from what to avoid.
verses.reflection: Verify your compass first thing today: do I actually know, right now, when to act and when to refrain?
verses.background: The promised account of the demonic nature begins here; Śrīdhara counts it as twelve verses. Krishna starts with what the demonic do not know: what to take up and what to turn away from.
verses.hook: What do people of demonic nature fail to understand?

views.text: Pravṛtti is what should be done as a means to human ends; nivṛtti is the evil one should turn from. Lacking both, the demonic are deceitful and given to lies.
They do not know Vedic dharma, the path to prosperity and to release. Purity is fitness for rites, and conduct means practices like twilight prayer, without which one stays unholy.
Takes pravṛtti and nivṛtti cosmically: the demonic know neither where the universe arises from nor into what it dissolves.
Lacking faith in scripture, the demonic cannot tell right from wrong; modern relativism that denies absolute truth shows how this leads to ethical chaos.

verses.devanagari:
असत्यमप्रतिष्ठं ते जगदाहुरनीश्वरम् ।
अपरस्परसम्भूतं किमन्यत्कामहैतुकम्॥
verses.transliteration:
asatyamapratiṣṭhaṃ te jagadāhuranīśvaram
aparasparasambhūtaṃ kimanyatkāmahaitukam
verses.essence: They say the world is without truth, without foundation, without God — born of mutual union, with desire for its cause; what else?
verses.translation: They say, "This universe is without truth, without (moral) basis, without a God, brought about by mutual union, with lust for its cause; what else?"

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, accusative singular (describes the world)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + सत्य (truth)
अ (without) + प्रतिष्ठा (foundation): having no foundation

anvaya.form: verb, perfect with present sense, 3rd person plural

anvaya.parts: अन् (without) + ईश्वर (Lord, ruler)
अपर (one) + पर (other) + सम्भूत (born): arisen from the union of male and female
काम (desire, lust) + हैतुक (having as cause): with lust as its cause

verses.explanation: The asuric creed, stated fairly before it is judged: no truth beneath appearances, no moral foundation, no Lord; the cosmos a chain of couplings driven by appetite — kim anyat, *what else could there be?* The shrug at the end is the signature. The Gita's objection is not to inquiry but to where this premise leads when lived: the next verses trace a worldview becoming a wake of destruction.
verses.connection: The philosophical seed (16.8) whose human harvest 16.9–20 will follow step by step.
verses.reflection: Notice where 'what else could there be?' has crept into your worldview — and reopen one window.
verses.background: Having said the demonic lack purity, conduct and truth, Krishna now reports their view of the world. Śrīdhara frames it as answering a question: how can anyone ignore right and wrong, or deny the God who made the world? Because of what they believe, given here in their own words.
verses.hook: How do the demonic describe the world and its origin?

views.text: 'Unreal' because the speakers, false themselves, see the world as false; 'baseless' because it rests on no dharma and adharma; 'godless' because no ruler apportions results. Lust is its only cause — the materialist view.
They deny that the world has Brahman, the True, for its self and its support, and deny that the Lord whose will is always true controls it.
Kim anyat: for them there is nothing beyond what is seen.

Asatya means there is no valid authority such as the Veda and Purāṇas for the world: they reject scripture, so they see the world's variety as simply natural, with no dharma behind it and no Lord making it.
Denying God lets the demonic escape moral restraint, so they explain the world as an accident without basis and treat lust, a distorted reflection of divine love, as life's purpose.

verses.devanagari:
एतां दृष्टिमवष्टभ्य नष्टात्मानोऽल्पबुद्धयः ।
प्रभवन्त्युग्रकर्माणः क्षयाय जगतोऽहिताः॥
verses.transliteration:
etāṃ dṛṣṭimavaṣṭabhya naṣṭātmāno'lpabuddhayaḥ
prabhavantyugrakarmāṇaḥ kṣayāya jagato'hitāḥ
verses.essence: Holding fast to this view, these lost souls of small understanding rise up as enemies of the world, of cruel deeds, for its destruction.
verses.translation: Holding this view, these ruined souls of small intellect and fierce deeds, come forth as the enemies of the world for its destruction.

anvaya.form: pronoun, feminine, accusative singular (agrees with दृष्टिम्)

anvaya.base: अव + √स्तम्भ् · to prop up, hold firm
नष्टात्मन् · one whose self is ruined
anvaya.parts: नष्ट (lost, ruined) + आत्मन् (self): those whose selves are ruined
अल्प (small) + बुद्धि (intellect): those whose understanding is small
उग्र (fierce, cruel) + कर्मन् (deed): those whose deeds are cruel
अ (not) + हित (friendly, beneficial)

verses.explanation: The chain from creed to deed: avaṣṭabhya — *clinging* to the view, leaning whole weight on it. If nothing is sacred and desire is the only engine, then ugra-karmāṇaḥ, ruthless action, becomes simply rational. Naṣṭātmānaḥ, the lost selves: the verse's pity inside its alarm — the world's destroyers are first of all people who have misplaced themselves.
verses.connection: 16.8's philosophy goes operational: ideas, the Gita insists, have body counts.
verses.reflection: Trace one idea you hold to its lived consequences today — philosophies have body counts.
verses.background: Krishna has just quoted the creed of the demonic: a world without truth, foundation or God, born of lust alone. Now he describes the people who hold that view and what they become when they act on it.
verses.hook: What happens when people of ruinous views gain strength?

views.text: Naṣṭātmānaḥ are those fallen from the disciplines that lead to the next world; their intellect is small because it is wholly taken up with material things.
Their selves are 'lost' because they do not grasp that the self, the knower, is different from the body, which is a known object like a jar.
'This view' is the Lokāyata (materialist) doctrine; holding it, their minds stained and fixed only on visible gains, they come into being as enemies for the world's ruin.
Rejecting the soul's eternity and karma, like the materialist Charvak, the demonic justify cruelty, and when they hold power, as tyrants have, they bring ruin to the world.

verses.devanagari:
काममाश्रित्य दुष्पूरं दम्भमानमदान्विताः ।
मोहाद्गृहीत्वासद्ग्राहान्प्रवर्तन्तेऽशुचिव्रताः॥
verses.transliteration:
kāmamāśritya duṣpūraṃ dambhamānamadānvitāḥ
mohādgṛhītvāsadgrāhānpravartante'śucivratāḥ
verses.essence: Surrendered to insatiable desire, full of hypocrisy, pride and intoxication, holding false notions through delusion, they act with impure resolves.
verses.translation: Filled with insatiable desires, full of hypocrisy, pride and arrogance, holding evil ideas through delusion, they work with impure resolves.

anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, accusative singular (agrees with कामम्)
anvaya.parts: दुस् (hard) + पूर (filling): impossible to fill

anvaya.base: दम्भमानमदान्वित · filled with hypocrisy, pride and intoxication
anvaya.parts: दम्भ (hypocrisy) + मान (pride) + मद (intoxication) + अन्वित (joined with): those filled with these

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, ablative singular (from, because of)

anvaya.parts: असत् (false, evil) + ग्राह (grasp, fixed idea): evil fixed ideas
अशुचि (impure) + व्रत (vow, resolve): those whose vows are impure

verses.explanation: The engine room: kāmam duṣpūram — desire that *cannot* be filled, a vessel with no bottom, taken as one's refuge (āśritya, the same word elsewhere used for taking refuge in God). The substitution is the whole tragedy: appetite installed in the throne meant for the eternal. Around it gather hypocrisy, pride, and mada, intoxication — drunk on self.
verses.connection: After the creed of 16.8 and the ruin of 16.9, the desire that drives it all: insatiable craving, pride and impure resolve.
verses.reflection: Find the bottomless vessel you keep refilling — and stop pouring for one day.
verses.background: The portrait moves from the creed to the desire that drives it. Śrīdhara reads this verse as describing such people turning to lesser deities and spells in pursuit of buried treasure and similar fantasies, which they seize on out of delusion.
verses.hook: What drives the actions of those with a demonic nature?

views.text: Given to insatiable passion and full of vanity, pride and arrogance, the demoniac adopt evil intentions out of delusion, meaning non-discrimination, and act in the world with impure resolves.
Their desires are for objects that cannot be had, and through ignorance they think such desires can be met only with wealth taken unlawfully; their vows are ones the Śāstras forbid.
Their false fixations are schemes like 'by this mantra I will propitiate that deity and win great treasures'; they worship petty powers, and their impure vows centre on wine and meat.
Dambha is pretending to righteousness, māna claiming honour one does not deserve, mada heaping greatness on oneself that one lacks; desire, like fire, grows the more it is fed.
Indulging insatiable desire makes their hearts impure and hypocritical, and pride convinces them no one is wiser, so they act against scripture and truth.

verses.devanagari:
चिन्तामपरिमेयां च प्रलयान्तामुपाश्रिताः ।
कामोपभोगपरमा एतावदिति निश्चिताः॥
verses.transliteration:
cintāmaparimeyāṃ ca pralayāntāmupāśritāḥ
kāmopabhogaparamā etāvaditi niścitāḥ
verses.essence: Beset by immeasurable cares ending only with death, holding the enjoyment of desire as the highest aim, convinced that this is all —
verses.translation: Giving themselves over to immeasurable cares ending only with death, regarding gratification of lust as their highest aim, and feeling sure that that is all.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + परिमेय (measurable)
प्रलय (death, dissolution) + अन्त (end): whose end is death

anvaya.base: कामोपभोगपरम · devoted to enjoyment above all
anvaya.parts: काम (desired things) + उपभोग (enjoyment) + परम (highest): for whom enjoying desires is the highest goal

verses.explanation: The inner weather of the creed: cintām aparimeyām, anxiety without measure, scheduled to end pralayāntām — only at death. The logic is airtight: if enjoyment is everything and time is short, then worry is the only rational state. Etāvad iti niścitāḥ — 'this much is all there is,' the certainty that closes every window. The portrait's cruelest detail: they are not enjoying it.
verses.connection: The cost accounting begins: the pleasure-creed billed in lifelong, terminal anxiety.
verses.reflection: Measure the creed by its weather today: where enjoyment is everything, anxiety is the climate.
verses.background: The description reaches the inner life of those who live by desire: worries without measure that end only at death. Śrīdhara notes that this verse runs straight into the next, where its sentence finds its verb, "they strive to amass wealth".
verses.hook: What do worldly people believe life is for, until death?

views.text: Kāma means the things desired, like sound and touch; they are convinced that enjoying these is the whole human goal, and are weighed down by cares too vast to estimate.
Sure to die today or tomorrow, they burden themselves with cares about things they could not obtain even by the time of death.
Reads pralayāntām as dissolution: their anxiety never ceases, because arising and dissolving never end.
Construes this verse with 'they strive to amass wealth' in the next, and links it to the Bārhaspatya (materialist) maxim that desire is the only human aim.

Chasing worldly gains brings endless anxiety from getting, keeping and losing; if the same concern went into loving God, one would cross beyond death, but the demonic see sense pleasure as the highest joy.

verses.devanagari:
आशापाशशतैर्बद्धाः कामक्रोधपरायणाः ।
ईहन्ते कामभोगार्थमन्यायेनार्थसञ्चयान्॥
verses.transliteration:
āśāpāśaśatairbaddhāḥ kāmakrodhaparāyaṇāḥ
īhante kāmabhogārthamanyāyenārthasañcayān
verses.essence: — bound by a hundred snares of hope, given over to desire and anger, they strive to amass wealth by wrongful means for the indulgence of desires.
verses.translation: Bound by a hundred ties of hope, given over to lust and anger, they strive to obtain by unlawful means hoards to wealth for sensual enjoyments.

anvaya.meaning: by hundreds of nooses of hope
anvaya.base: आशापाशशत · hundreds of snares of hope
anvaya.parts: आशा (hope) + पाश (noose) + शत (hundred): by hundreds of nooses that are hopes

anvaya.meaning: given over to desire and anger
anvaya.base: कामक्रोधपरायण · devoted to desire and anger
anvaya.parts: काम (desire) + क्रोध (anger) + परायण (final refuge): those whose refuge is desire and anger

anvaya.base: कामभोगार्थ · for the sake of enjoyment
anvaya.parts: काम (desire) + भोग (enjoyment) + अर्थ (purpose): for the purpose of enjoying desires

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, instrumental singular (by means of)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + न्याय (right method)
अर्थ (wealth) + सञ्चय (heap): heaps of wealth

verses.explanation: Āśā-pāśa-śataiḥ: hope itself as a hundred nooses — the asuric life is tied not by despair but by *expectation*, each anticipated pleasure another cord. Desire and its bodyguard anger (the old pair from 3.37) run the operation; anyāyena, by whatever bends, the wealth piles up. The verse paints acquisition as a form of bondage wearing the costume of success.
verses.connection: The behavioral output: craving plus deadline equals accumulation without scruple.
verses.reflection: Count your nooses of hope tonight — the expectations binding tomorrow before it arrives. Cut one.
verses.background: This verse completes the sentence begun in 16.11: those weighed down by endless cares, sure that enjoyment is all there is, now act on it. Śrīdhara opens it with "therefore": because they think so, they are pulled every way by hopes.
verses.hook: What drives people to gather wealth by any means, fair or foul?

refs.note: One may keep only the wealth needed for one's upkeep; hoarding more makes one a thief before God, deserving punishment, as those who gather wealth wrongly do.

views.text: The hopes themselves are the nooses, dragging them this way and that. They gather wealth by theft and the like, only for enjoyment and never for righteous acts.
Since gratification is their highest goal, anger arises the moment it is thwarted; that is why desire and anger are named together.
Hope binds a person to the wheel of saṃsāra like a rope; however much they own, their cravings multiply daily.
Money is the means of enjoyment, so desire-driven people chase it even unlawfully. They are punished twice: the wealth is taken at death, and the sins of earning it bring karmic consequences.

verses.devanagari:
इदमद्य मया लब्धमिमं प्राप्स्ये मनोरथम् ।
इदमस्तीदमपि मे भविष्यति पुनर्धनम्॥
verses.transliteration:
idamadya mayā labdhamimaṃ prāpsye manoratham
idamastīdamapi me bhaviṣyati punardhanam
verses.essence: 'This I have gained today; this longing I shall fulfill. This is mine — and this wealth too shall be mine.
verses.translation: "This has been gained by me today; this desire of mine I shall fulfil; this is mine and this wealth also shall be mine in future."

anvaya.form: pronoun, masculine, accusative singular (agrees with मनोरथम्)

anvaya.parts: मनस् (mind) + रथ (chariot): what the mind rides toward, a wish

anvaya.form: pronoun, short genitive singular (my, to me)

verses.explanation: The teaching changes register: for three verses (16.13–15) Krishna stops describing and starts *quoting* — the asuric inner monologue performed verbatim. Listen to the words: idam, mayā, idam, me — this, by me, this, mine. A grammar with one person in it. The eerie power of the passage is its familiarity; everyone has caught this voice running in their own head at 2 a.m.
verses.connection: The soliloquy begins: the demonic rendered not as other, but as a voice the reader recognizes.
verses.reflection: Catch the monologue running — this is mine, this too shall be mine — and simply hear its grammar.
verses.background: Krishna now lets the demonic speak for themselves. Śrīdhara says the four verses 16.13–16 give their daydream and then the hell it leads to; this verse opens the inner monologue with what was gained today and what comes next.
verses.hook: How does a greedy mind keep count of what it has and wants?

views.text: The monologue of plans: this is in hand, and next year that wealth too will come, and 'I shall be rich and famous'.
The key is 'by myself': land, sons and wealth gained solely by my own ability, with no help from any higher power or good fortune.
Calls these lines their 'mental kingdom', castles built in the mind; read with the next verses, they end in 16.16's fall into hell.
The demoniac assume a right to every pleasure and pursue it by any means, even through rituals. Their ego, fed by owning, hides a constant sense of not enough, and the cure is humility.

verses.devanagari:
असौ मया हतः शत्रुर्हनिष्ये चापरानपि ।
ईश्वरोऽहमहं भोगी सिद्धोऽहं बलवान्सुखी॥
verses.transliteration:
asau mayā hataḥ śatrurhaniṣye cāparānapi
īśvaro'hamahaṃ bhogī siddho'haṃ balavānsukhī
verses.essence: 'That enemy has been slain by me, and others too I shall slay. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am accomplished, mighty and happy.
verses.translation: "That enemy has been slain by me; and others also I shall slay. I am the lord. I enjoy. I am perfect, powerful and happy."
verses.explanation: The monologue crescendos into theology: īśvaro 'ham — *I am the Lord* — the title the Gita gives to the one now speaking, claimed by the deluded self. Every 'aham' is a small coronation: enjoyer, perfected, powerful, sukhī — happy, asserted rather than felt, the way one insists on what is slipping. The asura who called the world godless (16.8) ends by applying for the position.
verses.connection: The monologue's core: self-deification, the exact inversion of 15.18, where Krishna alone is declared the highest Person.
verses.reflection: When 'I am the lord' whispers in any costume today, smile and return the crown.
verses.background: The inner monologue of the demonic continues, moving from wealth to enemies and power. Having counted gains in 16.13, the speaker now boasts of the rival he has killed and those he will kill, and crowns himself lord.
verses.hook: How does a proud person boast after defeating an enemy?

views.text: Siddha means fulfilled in every way, blessed with sons and grandsons; the boast runs on: none is equal to me, others are only a burden on the earth.
Every claim is 'by myself': I am independent and ruler of others, successful and happy through my own powers. Destiny is dismissed as a fancy of weak minds.
Respecting only power, the demoniac harm others to clear their way and see themselves as lords and enjoyers. This ego is the great untruth of life, which every tradition urges us to dismantle.

verses.devanagari:
आढ्योऽभिजनवानस्मि कोऽन्योऽस्ति सदृशो मया ।
यक्ष्ये दास्यामि मोदिष्य इत्यज्ञानविमोहिताः॥
verses.transliteration:
āḍhyo'bhijanavānasmi ko'nyo'sti sadṛśo mayā
yakṣye dāsyāmi modiṣya ityajñānavimohitāḥ
verses.essence: 'I am wealthy and well-born — who else is equal to me? I shall sacrifice, I shall give, I shall rejoice.' Thus deluded by unknowing —
verses.translation: "I am rich and born in a noble family. Who else is equal to me? I shall perform sacrifices. I shall give (charity). I shall rejoice," thus deluded by ignorance.

anvaya.parts: अभिजन (lineage) + -वत् (having): having a noble lineage
अज्ञान (ignorance) + विमोहित (deluded): deluded by ignorance

verses.explanation: Even religion enters the inventory: yakṣye dāsyāmi — I *shall* sacrifice, I *shall* donate — piety scheduled as another acquisition, worship as self-decoration. Ko 'nyo 'sti sadṛśo mayā: 'who is like me?' — the question that, asked of God, is awe, and asked of oneself, is the whole disease. The quotation closes on its diagnosis: ajñāna-vimohitāḥ, all of it spoken inside a fog.
verses.connection: The soliloquy ends with piety itself annexed by ego — and 16.16 shows where the fog leads.
verses.reflection: Watch piety serve the ego once today — the announced donation, the displayed virtue — first in yourself.
verses.background: The last part of the monologue of the demonic: after wealth and conquest, family and even religious giving are claimed for the self. The words close with Krishna's own verdict, "deluded by ignorance", which carries into the next verse.
verses.hook: What makes the arrogant believe no one is equal to them?

views.text: Abhijanavān: seven generations of Vedic learning in the family. Even their sacrifice aims to outdo others, and their giving goes to actors and entertainers.
The ignorance is believing they can sacrifice, give and prosper by their own ability, without the grace of God.
They sacrifice to win more prestige than other initiated sacrificers and give to those who praise them; ignorance has set them in a false fixation.
Pride in birth and riches leads such people to feel they need not bow to God. Saints teach the opposite: grace flows, like water, to those who are low and unassuming.

verses.devanagari:
अनेकचित्तविभ्रान्ता मोहजालसमावृताः ।
प्रसक्ताः कामभोगेषु पतन्ति नरकेऽशुचौ॥
verses.transliteration:
anekacittavibhrāntā mohajālasamāvṛtāḥ
prasaktāḥ kāmabhogeṣu patanti narake'śucau
verses.essence: — led astray by many fancies, wrapped in a net of delusion, addicted to the gratification of desires, they fall into a foul hell.
verses.translation: Bewildered by many a fancy, entangled in the snare of delusion, addicted to the gratification of lust, they fall into a foul hell.

anvaya.parts: अनेक (many) + चित्त (thought) + विभ्रान्त (bewildered): bewildered by many schemes

anvaya.base: मोहजालसमावृत · enveloped in a net of delusion
anvaya.parts: मोह (delusion) + जाल (net) + समावृत (covered): wrapped in the net of delusion
काम (desire) + भोग (enjoyment)

anvaya.form: adjective, masculine, locative singular (agrees with नरके)

verses.explanation: The trajectory completes: aneka-citta-vibhrāntāḥ, a mind scattered across its own schemes; moha-jāla, delusion as a *net* — each strand thin, the weave inescapable. The fall into naraka needs no external judge; a life built on 16.13–15's monologue is already constructing its own descent, the way a spiral stair needs no one to push.
verses.connection: Where the monologue of 16.13–15 ends: a fall into hell, which 16.19–20 will describe as Krishna's own act.
verses.reflection: Find one strand of the self-woven net today — a scheme, a fantasy — and decline to add another.
verses.background: The sentence running through 16.13–15 reaches its end. Śrīdhara introduces it as "hear what such people come to": after three verses of their own boasts, Krishna says where they fall.
verses.hook: Where do restless, desire-bound thoughts finally lead a person?

refs.note: Action rules this world; whatever people do, they taste its fruit, so no one escapes the result of their deeds.
The sattvic rise, the rajasic stay in the middle, and the tamasic sink, matching the fall into hell this verse describes.

views.text: Moha is lack of discrimination; it is a net because it covers. Through the sins so gathered they fall into foul hells such as Vaitaraṇī.
Refusing to admit that past karma and the Lord play any part in their success, they are bewildered by plan after plan and die in the midst of their enjoyments.
They are scattered because they hold no conviction; the 'foul' place is both hell and the endless round of birth and death.
Their minds run in many directions after many wishes; the net is like a fisherman's, holding them as fish are held.

Ruled by the ego, people are possessed by repetitive negative thoughts such as complaint and grievance. Results come by God's law of karma, so those who cultivate demoniac qualities descend to lower states.

verses.devanagari:
आत्मसम्भाविताः स्तब्धा धनमानमदान्विताः ।
यजन्ते नामयज्ञैस्ते दम्भेनाविधिपूर्वकम्॥
verses.transliteration:
ātmasambhāvitāḥ stabdhā dhanamānamadānvitāḥ
yajante nāmayajñaiste dambhenāvidhipūrvakam
verses.essence: Self-honoring, stubborn, filled with the pride and intoxication of wealth, they perform sacrifices in name only, with hypocrisy, against all rule.
verses.translation: Self-conceited, stubborn, filled with the pride and intoxication of wealth, they perform sacrifices in name out of ostentation, contrary to scriptural ordinances.

anvaya.parts: आत्मन् (oneself) + सम्भावित (esteemed): esteemed only by themselves

anvaya.base: धनमानमदान्वित · filled with wealth's pride and intoxication
anvaya.parts: धन (wealth) + मान (pride) + मद (intoxication) + अन्वित (joined with): filled with the pride and intoxication of wealth

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, instrumental plural (with, by means of)
anvaya.parts: नामन् (name) + यज्ञ (sacrifice): a sacrifice only in name, or for a name
अ (not) + विधि (rule) + पूर्वक (according to): not done by the prescribed rule

verses.explanation: The religious performance examined: nāma-yajñaiḥ — sacrifices in name only, ritual as theater, the donation announced, the temple wing named after the donor. Ātma-sambhāvitāḥ: honored by themselves — having appointed themselves their own audience and judge, applause is guaranteed. Worship without surrender is the asuric creed's most refined costume.
verses.connection: Returns to 16.15's 'I shall sacrifice' and shows the performance up close.
verses.reflection: Do one good thing today with no audience at all — not even the inner one applauding.
verses.background: Śrīdhara says Krishna returns to the boast "I shall sacrifice" from 16.15 to show that such sacrifice is driven by display and ego, not by goodness. This verse and the next describe how the demonic actually worship.
verses.hook: Why does a lavish ritual done for show earn no merit?

refs.note: Advertising a good deed lessens its merit, while keeping it secret multiplies it, which is why showy sacrifice is empty.

views.text: Self-esteemed means thinking themselves virtuous when holy men do not; the sacrifices lack the subsidiary rites and proper procedure.
Nāma-yajña is sacrifice done for fame, to be known as a great sacrificer; regarding themselves as already perfect, they do nothing real.
Offers a second reading: sacrifices done only to earn a title such as 'Dīkṣita' or 'Somayājī'. They are offered with hypocrisy instead of faith.
The demoniac also sacrifice, but to look pious and advertise themselves, ignoring scriptural rules. Such rituals done for display are dismissed as incorrectly performed.

verses.devanagari:
अहंकारं बलं दर्पं कामं क्रोधं च संश्रिताः ।
मामात्मपरदेहेषु प्रद्विषन्तोऽभ्यसूयकाः॥
verses.transliteration:
ahaṃkāraṃ balaṃ darpaṃ kāmaṃ krodhaṃ ca saṃśritāḥ
māmātmaparadeheṣu pradviṣanto'bhyasūyakāḥ
verses.essence: Clinging to ego, force, arrogance, desire and anger, these malicious ones hate me in their own bodies and in those of others.
verses.translation: Given over to egoism, power, haughtiness, lust and anger, these malicious people hate Me in their own bodies and in those of others.

anvaya.parts: अहम् (I) + कार (making): the sense of 'I am the doer'

anvaya.meaning: in their own and others' bodies
anvaya.base: आत्मपरदेह · one's own and others' bodies
anvaya.parts: आत्मन् (oneself) + पर (others) + देह (body): in their own bodies and those of others

anvaya.base: अभ्यसूयक · one who finds fault with the good

verses.explanation: The portrait's theological depth-charge: mām ātma-para-deheṣu pradviṣantaḥ — they hate *me*, dwelling in their own bodies and in everyone else's. Every cruelty to another and every violence to oneself is, by chapter 15's indwelling doctrine, aimed at the same resident. No one has ever harmed a creature without the blow landing on God.
verses.connection: Links the demonic life to 15.15's Lord seated in every heart: their hatred of others is finally hatred of him.
verses.reflection: Remember the address of every cruelty today: the same resident, in your body and in theirs.
verses.background: Krishna is still describing the showy sacrifices of the demonic. Śrīdhara reads this verse as expanding "contrary to rule" from 16.17: in rites without faith they harm themselves and the creatures they offer, and so hate the Lord present in every body.
verses.hook: Whom do the envious really hate when they hate others?

views.text: Hating Me means transgressing My commands; I dwell in their bodies and others' as witness of intellect and action. Abhyasūyakāḥ: they cannot bear the virtues of those on the right path.
Ego says 'I can do everything without anyone's help'. Unable to tolerate the Supreme Person within them and others, they invent arguments against His existence.
Because the Lord dwells everywhere, in hating other people they hate Him alone, and acting against their own self they bring about their own fall.
Continues the faithless sacrifice of 16.17: torturing the body in rites without faith, and killing animals against the rule, harm the conscious Lord who dwells in those bodies; that is the 'hatred'.
Such people find fault in all, envy others' success and rage when opposed. In doing so they disrespect the Supreme Soul who dwells in their own hearts and in everyone else's.

verses.devanagari:
तानहं द्विषतः क्रूरान्संसारेषु नराधमान् ।
क्षिपाम्यजस्रमशुभानासुरीष्वेव योनिषु॥
verses.transliteration:
tānahaṃ dviṣataḥ krūrānsaṃsāreṣu narādhamān
kṣipāmyajasramaśubhānāsurīṣveva yoniṣu
verses.essence: These cruel haters, worst of men — I hurl them again and again into demonic wombs alone, in the cycles of birth and death.
verses.translation: Those cruel haters, worst among men in the world, I hurl those evil-doers into the wombs of demons only.

anvaya.parts: नर (man) + अधम (lowest): the lowest among men
अ (not) + शुभ (auspicious)

anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, locative plural (agrees with योनिषु)

verses.explanation: The hardest verse in the chapter, and tradition reads its verb with care: kṣipāmi, 'I hurl,' is the Lord speaking as the law of consequence itself — the same impartiality of 9.29 ('I am alike to all') seen from its stern face. Like gravitates to like: a consciousness drenched in cruelty is drawn to births where cruelty is the native climate. No caprice, no vendetta — trajectory, owned by the one who upholds all trajectories.
verses.connection: Consequence personified: 14.18's downward pull, spoken in the first person.
verses.reflection: Catch one small cruelty in your speech or thoughts today and replace it once with its opposite; the verse warns that such habits deepen themselves.
verses.background: The account of the demonic turns to its result, spoken by Krishna in the first person. Śrīdhara introduces 16.19–20 as saying that such people never fall away from their demonic nature; this verse names what the Lord himself does with them.
verses.hook: What becomes of the cruel and hateful in their next births?

views.text: Because of their own unrighteousness the Lord casts them, for ever, into demonic species such as tigers and lions, full of evil deeds.
The hurling means joining them to cruel minds that drive them to actions leading to accursed births, births that turn them away from any friendliness toward the Lord.
They never fall away from their demonic nature; 'I hurl' means 'I give their sinful acts exactly such a fruit'.
'For ever' means only until they purify their hearts; there is no such thing as eternal damnation.
God, not the soul, decides the next birth according to one's nature and karma. Those with demoniac minds are placed in families and species that suit and express that nature.

verses.devanagari:
आसुरीं योनिमापन्ना मूढा जन्मनि जन्मनि ।
मामप्राप्यैव कौन्तेय ततो यान्त्यधमां गतिम्॥
verses.transliteration:
āsurīṃ yonimāpannā mūḍhā janmani janmani
māmaprāpyaiva kaunteya tato yāntyadhamāṃ gatim
verses.essence: Entering demonic wombs, deluded birth after birth, failing to reach me, Kaunteya, they sink to the lowest state.
verses.translation: Entering into demoniacal wombs and deluded, birth after birth, not attaining Me, they thus fall, O Arjuna, into a condition still lower than that.

anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, accusative singular (agrees with योनिम्)
past participle, masculine, nominative plural (as noun: the deluded)
noun, neuter, locative singular (repeated: birth after birth)
adjective, feminine, accusative singular (agrees with गतिम्)

verses.explanation: The descent's full arc, and its hardest word: mām aprāpya eva, 'never reaching me.' Śaṅkara and Śrīdhara read the eva as emphatic: there is no question of reaching the Lord here; what these lives fail to reach is even the path that leads to him, so each birth sinks lower than the last (tataḥ adhamām). Sivananda softens 16.19's 'for ever' to 'until the heart is purified.' And the chapter does not stop at the bottom: the next two verses name the three doors, and the way out through them.
verses.connection: Bottom of the descent — with the exit deliberately left unbarred, as 16.21–22 confirms.
verses.reflection: Notice one pattern in yourself that gets worse each time you repeat it, and name it plainly today, before another round.
verses.background: Following on from 16.19, where Krishna says he casts the cruel into demonic births, this verse traces them through birth after birth. Śrīdhara stresses "not attaining Me": they never even find the good path toward him, and sink lower still.
verses.hook: What is the final end of those who never turn toward God?

views.text: Since reaching the Lord is out of the question for them, 'not reaching Me' means not reaching even the virtuous path He enjoins; they sink into states still lower.
Never coming to know that Vāsudeva, Lord and ruler of all, truly exists, they take births ever more hostile to Him and go further and further down.
Hating others is hating Vāsudeva, who dwells everywhere; hostile to their own Self, they act for their own fall.
The way out is to destroy these tendencies by cultivating the divine qualities and by regular meditation; only then comes liberation.
Birth after birth in degraded settings only deepens a demoniac nature. Failing to reach God, such souls sink even to lowly creatures, receptacles for the evil-minded.

verses.devanagari:
त्रिविधं नरकस्येदं द्वारं नाशनमात्मनः ।
कामः क्रोधस्तथा लोभस्तस्मादेतत्त्रयं त्यजेत्॥
verses.transliteration:
trividhaṃ narakasyedaṃ dvāraṃ nāśanamātmanaḥ
kāmaḥ krodhastathā lobhastasmādetattrayaṃ tyajet
verses.essence: Threefold is this gate of hell, destructive of the self: desire, anger, and greed. Therefore let one abandon these three.
verses.translation: Triple is the gate of this hell, destructive of the self lust, anger and greed; therefore one should abandon these three.

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, nominative singular (agrees with द्वारम्)
anvaya.parts: त्रि (three) + विधा (kind): of three kinds

anvaya.form: pronoun, neuter, accusative singular (agrees with त्रयम्)

verses.explanation: After fourteen verses of portrait, the practical distillation: tri-vidhaṃ narakasya dvāram — hell has three doors, kāma, krodha, lobha: desire, anger, greed. Śaṅkara notes that merely entering them ruins the self, leaving it unfit for any human goal. The whole demonic catastrophe of 16.7–20, traced back, passes through one of these three hinges, and they open from the inside. The instruction is correspondingly finite: tasmād etat trayaṃ tyajet, drop these three, and the whole edifice loses its foundation. Diagnosis becomes doorkeeping.
verses.connection: The chapter's actionable core: the vast darkness reduced to three guarded doors.
verses.reflection: Guard the three doors today by name: one craving declined, one anger cooled, one grasping opened.
verses.background: The long portrait of the demonic is complete. Śaṅkara introduces this verse as a summary of all those traits, countless as they are, gathered under three, so that avoiding the three avoids them all. Krishna now names that gate.
verses.hook: Which three passions open the door to self-destruction?

views.text: By merely entering this door the self is ruined: it becomes unfit for any human goal. The verse is a praise of renouncing these three.
Dvāra means the path, the cause: these three are the cause of that dreadful hell, so they must be wholly given up.
Of all the demonic faults described, these three are the root of every fault, which is why they alone are singled out to be abandoned completely.
Lust, anger and greed are the roots of every demoniac vice, with anger and greed both growing out of lust. One who wants welfare should dread them and keep them out of one's personality.

verses.devanagari:
एतैर्विमुक्तः कौन्तेय तमोद्वारैस्त्रिभिर्नरः ।
आचरत्यात्मनः श्रेयस्ततो याति परां गतिम्॥
verses.transliteration:
etairvimuktaḥ kaunteya tamodvāraistribhirnaraḥ
ācaratyātmanaḥ śreyastato yāti parāṃ gatim
verses.essence: One who is released from these three gates of darkness, Kaunteya, practices what is good for the self — and so reaches the supreme goal.
verses.translation: A man who is liberated from these three gates to darkness, O Arjuna, practises what is good for him and thus goes to the Supreme Goal.

anvaya.form: pronoun, neuter, instrumental plural (from, with विमुक्तः)

anvaya.parts: तमस् (darkness) + द्वार (gate): gates leading to darkness

anvaya.form: noun, masculine, genitive singular (of, for the self)
adjective, feminine, accusative singular (agrees with गतिम्)

verses.explanation: The positive corollary, with a quiet insight tucked inside: ācaraty ātmanaḥ śreyaḥ — only *after* release from the three does one even begin practicing one's own true good. Desire, anger and greed do not merely cause suffering; they impersonate the self's interests so well that genuine self-care is impossible while they govern. Freedom from them is where real life starts.
verses.connection: Mirror of 16.21: the three doors closed, the road of the whole Gita reopens.
verses.reflection: Notice what genuine self-care becomes possible the hour the three doormen are off duty.
verses.background: Having named desire, anger and greed as the gate of hell and told Arjuna to abandon them, Krishna now says what follows for the one who does. Śrīdhara introduces the verse as the particular reward of that renunciation.
verses.hook: What opens up once desire, anger and greed are left behind?

views.text: Blocked by these three, one could not strive before; once they are gone one strives for the good and gains Liberation, and happiness here as well. Scripture is the means to both.
The three cause false knowledge about the Lord; freed of them, one comes to know Him, turns toward Him, and reaches the supreme goal, which is the Lord Himself.
'Practising one's good' means practising the means to it, such as austerity and yoga; from that comes liberation.

While these three remain, one chases pleasure that is sweet now and bitter later. Freed of them, the intellect chooses the good that is hard at first but sweet in the end, and moves toward the supreme goal.

verses.devanagari:
यः शास्त्रविधिमुत्सृज्य वर्तते कामकारतः ।
न स सिद्धिमवाप्नोति न सुखं न परां गतिम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yaḥ śāstravidhimutsṛjya vartate kāmakārataḥ
na sa siddhimavāpnoti na sukhaṃ na parāṃ gatim
verses.essence: One who casts aside the ordinances of scripture and acts by the impulse of desire attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
verses.translation: He who, having cast aside the ordinances of the scriptures, acts under the impulse of desire, attains not perfection, nor happiness nor the Supreme Goal.

anvaya.parts: शास्त्र (scripture) + विधि (injunction): the rule laid down by scripture
काम (desire) + कार (doing): doing as desire dictates

anvaya.form: adjective, feminine, accusative singular (agrees with गतिम्)

verses.explanation: The closing argument: why śāstra at all? Because kāma-kārataḥ — 'desire-driven' — is the only alternative compass, and the chapter has just spent fourteen verses showing where it navigates. Scripture here is not arbitrary command but a measure outside oneself; for Rāmānuja it is the Lord's own injunction, the Veda. Discarding the map, one steers by appetite — and appetite, 16.10 said, can never be filled: no perfection, no happiness, no supreme goal.
verses.connection: Grounds the chapter's ethics: without a measure beyond desire, 16.13's monologue becomes the only voice.
verses.reflection: Ask of one impulse today: is this guided by anything beyond appetite? If not, consult the map.
verses.background: Śrīdhara says giving up desire and the rest does not happen without following one's own duty, and this verse makes that point. After describing the freed person in 16.22, Krishna turns to the one who throws aside scripture's rule and acts on desire.
verses.hook: What do you lose by ignoring scripture and following every impulse?

views.text: Śāstra is the source of knowing duty and non-duty, as injunction and prohibition. Siddhi is fitness for Liberation; sukha is happiness even in this world.
Śāstra means the Vedas, the Lord's own injunction; abandoning it, one gains no attainment hereafter and not the slightest happiness here.
Giving up desire and the rest is impossible without doing one's own dharma; siddhi here is knowledge of truth and sukha is inner calm.
Scriptures are guide maps, telling what to do and what not to do. Those who reverse them and follow their whims gain neither true knowledge, nor real happiness, nor liberation.

verses.devanagari:
तस्माच्छास्त्रं प्रमाणं ते कार्याकार्यव्यवस्थितौ ।
ज्ञात्वा शास्त्रविधानोक्तं कर्म कर्तुमिहार्हसि॥
verses.transliteration:
tasmācchāstraṃ pramāṇaṃ te kāryākāryavyavasthitau
jñātvā śāstravidhānoktaṃ karma kartumihārhasi
verses.essence: Therefore let scripture be your measure in determining what is to be done and what is not. Knowing what the scriptural rule declares, you should act in this world.
verses.translation: Therefore, let the scripture be thy authority in determining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. Having known what is said in the ordinance of the scriptures, thou shouldst act here in this world.

anvaya.base: प्रमाण · measure, means of valid knowledge
anvaya.form: noun, neuter, nominative singular (what scripture is)

anvaya.meaning: in deciding right and wrong action
anvaya.base: कार्याकार्यव्यवस्थिति · settling what to do and not do
anvaya.parts: कार्य (to be done) + अकार्य (not to be done) + व्यवस्थिति (determination): in determining what should and should not be done

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, accusative singular (agrees with कर्म)
anvaya.parts: शास्त्र (scripture) + विधान (rule) + उक्त (stated): what is stated by the rule of scripture

verses.explanation: The chapter ends not in fear but in orientation: tasmāc chāstraṃ pramāṇaṃ te — let scripture be your measure. Pramāṇa is a means of valid knowing: desire measures everything by appetite, the asura by self, and the seeker needs a standard outside both, because kāma-kārataḥ has just been shown navigating to ruin. The commentators read the line firmly: for Rāmānuja the śāstra is the only authority, and Abhinavagupta warns against settling right and wrong by one's own reasoning. Jñātvā… kartum arhasi: know, then act. The Gita itself will end (18.63) by telling Arjuna to reflect fully and then do as he chooses.
verses.connection: Closes the two-natures teaching with a compass — and opens ch17's question: what of those who act in faith beyond the rules?
verses.reflection: Keep a measure outside your moods today — let something steadier than desire settle one decision.
verses.background: The chapter ends here. Having said that whoever sets aside scripture's rule gains neither perfection, happiness nor the goal, Krishna draws the conclusion for Arjuna himself. Śrīdhara calls this verse the result of the whole argument.
verses.hook: How can you know what you should and should not do?

refs.note: Every spiritual principle, past, present or future, must be established on the basis of the Vedas, which is why scripture is the measure of action.

views.text: Pramāṇa is the means of knowing what to do and avoid, as precepts 'do this', 'do not do that'. 'Here' marks the sphere in which one is entitled to act.
Śāstra, the Vedas supplemented by Dharma-śāstras, Itihāsas and Purāṇas, is the only authority; its enjoined acts are means of reaching and pleasing the Supreme Person.
Whoever rejects the injunctions and decides by his own intellect what to do falls; so do not settle right and wrong by your own reasoning.
Act according to your own entitlement, because purity of mind, right knowledge and liberation all have scripture for their root.
Following the heart is not enough, since the heart can mislead. The Vedic scriptures are the final authority on right action, so one should understand them and act by them.
